plates.reference: Own code graphic: on period paper, an inked Hayflick division limit & telomere shortening chart from Hayflick & Moorhead (December 1961 Exp. Cell Res. 25: 585–621), Blackburn & Gall (March 1978 J. Mol. Biol. 120: 33–53), and Greider & Blackburn (December 1985 Cell 43: 405–413) plots human telomere length (~10–15 kb of TTAGGG repeats at birth) dropping with each cell doubling until hitting the Hayflick senescence threshold at ~50 divisions (~4–5 kb), contrasted with germ cells, stem cells, and cancer cells maintaining telomere length via telomerase.

teach_overlay.label: 10–15 KB TTAGGG REPEATS AT BIRTH (−50–200 BP/DIVISION) → ~50 DIVISIONS HAYFLICK LIMIT VS TELOMERASE EXTENSION
teach_overlay.detail: Inked human telomere attrition & Hayflick limit chart on period paper showing human chromosome ends starting with ~10,000–15,000 base pairs of TTAGGG repeats at birth, losing ~50–200 base pairs per cell division across ~50 doublings (the Hayflick Limit) down to the ~4,000-bp senescence barrier, while telomerase rebuilds TTAGGG repeats in germ and stem cells
teach_overlay.scale: each of your forty-six chromosomes starts life with a protective DNA fuse about ten thousand letters long — and every time a cell divides, up to two hundred letters burn off the tip until after fifty divisions the fuse runs out
